module_title: Semiconductor Physics and p-n Junction (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level establishes the atomic and energetic basis of solid-state electronics. It thoroughly explores Energy Band Theory, the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, the mechanics of doping, and the formation of the p-n junction, which is the cornerstone of all modern electronic devices.

core_concepts.title: Energy Band Theory of Solids
core_concepts.description: In a crystal lattice, the closely packed atoms cause individual electron energy levels to merge into continuous bands. 1. Valence Band (VB): The highest energy band completely or partially filled with valence electrons. 2. Conduction Band (CB): The band immediately above the VB; electrons here are free to conduct current. 3. Forbidden Energy Gap ($E_g$): The energy separation between the VB and CB where no allowed electron states exist. For conductors, $E_g \approx 0$ (bands overlap). For insulators, $E_g > 3 \text{ eV}$. For semiconductors (Si, Ge), $E_g \approx 1 \text{ eV}$.

core_concepts.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
core_concepts.description: Intrinsic semiconductors are highly pure crystals (like pure Si or Ge) where thermal excitation creates equal numbers of electrons and holes ($n_e = n_h = n_i$). Their conductivity is too low for practical use. To increase conductivity, specific impurities are added (Doping), creating Extrinsic semiconductors. Even after doping, the Mass Action Law holds strictly true at thermal equilibrium: $n_e \cdot n_h = n_i^2$.

core_concepts.title: n-type and p-type Semiconductors
core_concepts.description: n-type: Formed by doping with Pentavalent impurities (P, As, Sb). Four valence electrons form covalent bonds, while the fifth is loosely bound and easily 'donated' to the conduction band. Electrons are the majority charge carriers ($n_e \gg n_h$). p-type: Formed by doping with Trivalent impurities (B, Al, In). The impurity has only three valence electrons, leaving a vacancy or 'hole' that can 'accept' an electron. Holes are the majority charge carriers ($n_h \gg n_e$).

core_concepts.title: Formation of p-n Junction & Depletion Layer
core_concepts.description: When a p-type and n-type semiconductor are joined at the atomic level, a concentration gradient causes majority carriers to diffuse across the junction (electrons move p-ward, holes move n-ward). This leaves behind immobile positive donor ions on the n-side and negative acceptor ions on the p-side, forming a 'Depletion Layer' devoid of mobile carriers. The electric field established by these ions creates a Barrier Potential ($V_b$) ($\approx 0.7 \text{ V}$ for Si, $\approx 0.3 \text{ V}$ for Ge) which halts further diffusion.

core_concepts.title: Biasing the p-n Junction
core_concepts.description: Forward Bias: The p-side is connected to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal of a battery. The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, shrinking the depletion layer and allowing a large exponential forward current to flow. Reverse Bias: The p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive. The applied voltage aids the barrier potential, widening the depletion layer. Only a tiny 'leakage current' flows due to minority carriers.

important_entities.name: The 'Hole'
important_entities.key_fact: A virtual positive charge representing the absence of an electron in a covalent bond.
important_entities.significance: A hole is not a physical particle; it is a mathematical and physical convenience to describe the collective movement of valence electrons jumping from bond to bond. Crucially, the mobility of a hole is always LESS than the mobility of a free electron because holes must navigate through the constrained valence band, whereas free electrons move in the relatively empty conduction band.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive conceptual trap: In metallic conductors, increasing temperature increases lattice vibrations, increasing collisions, which INCREASES resistance (Positive Temperature Coefficient). However, in semiconductors, increasing temperature breaks covalent bonds, exponentially generating new electron-hole pairs. The dramatic increase in charge carriers heavily overrides the collision effect, causing the resistance to DECREASE (Negative Temperature Coefficient).

Students frequently assume that an 'n-type' (negative type) semiconductor has a net negative charge, and a 'p-type' has a net positive charge. This is absolutely false. All extrinsic semiconductors are Electrically Neutral overall. The impurity atoms added during doping (like Arsenic or Boron) are themselves electrically neutral atoms.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To remember the trivalent dopants (which create p-type material): B (Boron), Al (Aluminum), Ga (Gallium), In (Indium). To remember the pentavalent dopants (which create n-type material): P (Phosphorus), As (Arsenic), Sb (Antimony), Bi (Bismuth).

exam_strategy_tips: In generic circuit problems involving p-n junction diodes, always check the biasing first. If the diode is stated as 'Ideal' and is Reverse Biased, physically erase it from your circuit diagram and leave it as an Open Circuit (broken wire). If it is Forward Biased, replace it with a plain connecting wire (Short Circuit) and apply standard Ohm's law/Kirchhoff's rules.
